clue.text: Tempestuous, like Lady Georgiana's life

definitions.meaning: wild and turbulent, as weather or a temper can be
Lady Georgiana Spencer, Duchess of Devonshire, led a famously turbulent life of scandal and debt

explanation.surface: A turbulent existence is compared to that of an aristocratic Georgian lady.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses mean full of upheaval: a tempest is a storm, and a life of scandal is a storm-tossed one.

clue.text: Hidden themes in books about U-boats?

indicators.note: books about a subject sit beside it, so the books word follows the boats word

parts.note: U-boats were German submarines, and a submarine is a sub
books are texts

explanation.surface: A reader wonders whether war stories about submarines carry deeper meanings.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'books about U-boats' is read literally: texts on subs.
explanation.definitionFit: Underlying meanings that lie beneath the obvious text of a work are what critics call by this word.

clue.text: Gifts for Odette Swann, denied Miss Blandish

definitions.meaning: in Proust, Swann courts Odette with cattleyas, a kind of these flowers
James Hadley Chase's thriller is titled No ___ for Miss Blandish

explanation.surface: Presents go to one literary heroine but are withheld from another.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattleyas are exotic flowers of this family, and Chase's title refuses the same blooms to his heroine.

clue.text: Upset main Latin character in Nicholas Nickleby

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and thrown into disorder, so the letters of the next two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some Latin text is overturned to reveal a figure from a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' rearranges MAIN and LATIN together into the Dickens name.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Mantalini is the dandyish husband of the dressmaker Madame Mantalini in Dickens's novel.

clue.text: Two months (one unsettled, one clear) to find Louisa M's youngest

indicators.note: unsettled means disturbed from its order, so the first month's letters are shuffled

parts.note: May is a month of the year
March is another month

explanation.surface: A calendar puzzle in which two months, one jumbled and one left intact, lead to a famous girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two months' gives MAY and MARCH; 'unsettled' scrambles MAY to AMY while 'clear' says MARCH stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Louisa May Alcott's Little Women has four sisters, of whom Amy is the youngest.

clue.text: Notice physicist providing nom de plume for novelist

parts.note: to notice is to mark
Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who split the atom

explanation.surface: Spotting a famous scientist's name used as a writer's pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hale White published his novels under this assumed name, a pen-name.

clue.text: Time's accompanies dance in roman fleuve

definitions.text: Time's accompanies dance in roman fleuve

parts.words: Time's accompanies dance in roman fleuve
parts.note: Anthony Powell's twelve-novel sequence, a roman-fleuve (printed here as 'veuve'), is A Dance to the ___ of Time, so the missing word goes with the dance and belongs to Time

explanation.surface: Something belonging to Time keeps company with a dance in a long sequence of novels.
explanation.walkthrough: A roman-fleuve is a novel sequence; Powell's title supplies the word that Time owns and that accompanies the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: In Powell's title the dance is set to the strains of Time's melody, the art of organised sound.

clue.text: "I'd like to see a Tank come down the stalls, / Lurching to - —— tunes" (Siegfried Sassoon)

definitions.text: "I'd like to see a Tank come down the stalls, / Lurching to - —— tunes" (Siegfried Sassoon)

parts.words: "I'd like to see a Tank come down the stalls, / Lurching to - —— tunes" (Siegfried Sassoon)
parts.note: Sassoon's poem Blighters imagines a tank crushing a music-hall audience as it lurches to the syncopated popular tunes of the day

explanation.surface: A quotation from a war poet with a gap to fill.
explanation.definitionFit: Syncopated popular piano music of the early twentieth century is the style the music-hall tunes belonged to.

clue.text: American name, said to be composer

indicators.note: said to be signals that the word for an American name is spoken, giving a composer's name of the same sound

parts.note: a handle is US slang for a name or nickname, as in CB radio

explanation.surface: An American's name turns out to belong to a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said to be' makes HANDLE, American slang for a name, sound like the composer of Messiah.
explanation.definitionFit: George Frideric Handel was the German-born composer of Messiah who worked in London.

clue.text: Character of 5 required then cue Frazier, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words might be arranged some other way, so the letters of the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A character from a novel is sought, perhaps via a cue to someone called Frazier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges THEN CUE FRAZIER; '5' points to the 5-down pen-name, whose novel Catharine Furze names this heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: The title heroine of Mark Rutherford's 1893 novel, a figure in that author's fiction.

clue.text: Cut short objection to mythical creature in ceremonial vessel

indicators.note: cut short means docked of its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a but is an objection, as in 'no buts'
a centaur is the half-man, half-horse of Greek myth

explanation.surface: Objecting to a mythical beast found aboard a grand ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'objection' is a noun here, as in 'no ifs or buts'; 'Cut short' docks its last letter. The vessel is the Venetian Doge's barge.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bucentaur was the Doge of Venice's state barge, used in the annual marriage-of-the-sea ceremony.

clue.text: Long narrative on Newton from French author

indicators.note: in a down or across sense the story sits on, that is next to, the newton letter

parts.note: a saga is a long story
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

explanation.surface: A lengthy story about Isaac Newton by a French writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newton' looks like the scientist but is the unit, symbol N.
explanation.definitionFit: Françoise Sagan was the French novelist of Bonjour Tristesse.

clue.text: "And were an — to be my story,/ I'd have a short one ready for my own" (Robert Frost)

definitions.text: "And were an — to be my story,/ I'd have a short one ready for my own" (Robert Frost)

parts.words: "And were an — to be my story,/ I'd have a short one ready for my own" (Robert Frost)
parts.note: Frost's The Lesson for Today ends by proposing the words for his own gravestone, 'I had a lover's quarrel with the world'

explanation.surface: A quotation from an American poet with a gap to fill.
explanation.definitionFit: Frost's short story for his own grave is a tombstone inscription.

clue.text: Lie like Goya's Maja

definitions.meaning: to lie is to lean back or lie at rest
Goya's paintings La Maja desnuda and La Maja vestida show a woman stretched out on a couch

explanation.surface: Comparing someone's posture to a famous Spanish painting.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying back at rest is the pose of the stretched-out woman in Goya's two Majas.

clue.text: British composer is into its complications

parts.note: the setter's slip: the anagram needs the word 'to', so only the TO of 'into' is fodder

indicators.note: complications are tangles, so the letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A composer gets drawn into the intricacies of something.
explanation.walkthrough: As printed, 'into its' has seven letters; the anagram signalled by 'complications' works only on TO ITS, so 'into' looks like a slip for 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Paolo Tosti, Italian-born, became a British subject and was knighted for his songs.

clue.text: Instrumental passage from Little Dorrit or Nelly's Version

indicators.note: from says the answer is taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Taking a passage of music from Dickens or from Eva Figes's novel Nelly's Version.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'DorRIT OR NELly's'; the book titles are misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: A ritornello is a recurring instrumental refrain between vocal passages.

clue.text: Mr Presley is not quite sure as stage manager

parts.note: Reg Presley was the singer of the 1960s band the Troggs

indicators.note: not quite right means slightly off, so the letters of the next word are disordered

explanation.surface: Elvis apparently is unsure about running the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr Presley' wants to be Elvis; it is Reg of the Troggs. 'not quite' rearranges SURE as SEUR.
explanation.definitionFit: In ballet and theatre the régisseur is the person who directs or manages the staging.

clue.text: A woman in love

parts.note: read as a reference to D.H. Lawrence's novel Women in Love, whose heroines Ursula and Gudrun share one surname

explanation.definitionFit: Ursula and Gudrun, the sisters at the centre of Lawrence's Women in Love, carry this family name.

clue.text: Gilbert's solitary game

definitions.meaning: one of Gilbert and Sullivan's comic operas has this title
a card game played alone, also called solitaire

explanation.surface: A librettist plays cards on his own.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta and the British name for the one-player card game.

clue.text: The signs may well be grave, if not acute

definitions.text: The signs may well be grave, if not acute

parts.words: The signs may well be grave, if not acute
parts.note: grave and acute read like medical or serious states, but they are marks placed over letters

explanation.definitionFit: Grave and acute are diacritical marks over vowels, as in French.

clue.text: Greek always poetically describes feminist writer

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: A Greek forever writes about a feminist.
explanation.definitionFit: Germaine Greer wrote The Female Eunuch, a key text of second-wave feminism.

clue.text: It describes part of speech

parts.note: read as a descriptive word or phrase, a part of speech that qualifies a person or thing

explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive adjective or byname added to a name, like 'the Great', serves as a describing term.

clue.text: He wrote 12 for a spy

parts.note: the 12-across word plus 'for a Spy' is the title of a 1938 thriller by an English spy novelist

explanation.definitionFit: Eric Ambler, the English thriller writer, wrote the 1938 novel whose title begins with the 12-across word.

clue.text: Avenging regicide of Fife

parts.note: in Shakespeare's Scottish play the Thane of Fife kills the murderous king to avenge his family

explanation.definitionFit: The Thane of Fife in Macbeth kills the usurping king, avenging the slaughter of his wife and children.

clue.text: A wave of the arms

parts.note: arms here are coats of arms, so the phrase means the heraldic term for a wavy line

explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry a line or band drawn in waves is described with this term.

clue.text: Margery Allingham set one in winding sheets

definitions.text: Margery Allingham set one in winding sheets

parts.words: Margery Allingham set one in winding sheets
parts.note: winding sheets are shrouds, and Allingham's 1938 detective novel is The ___ in Shrouds

explanation.definitionFit: Allingham's Campion novel set in the couture world is The Fashion in Shrouds, a winding sheet being a shroud.

clue.text: Apartment thus shelved suggests a Powell title

definitions.text: Apartment thus shelved suggests a Powell title

parts.words: Apartment thus shelved suggests a Powell title
parts.note: Powell's novel Books Do Furnish a Room implies a room whose walls are covered with shelves of books

explanation.definitionFit: A room furnished with shelves of books is said to be book-covered along its walls.

clue.text: Spectacle of new war heroes

indicators.note: new means remade, so the letters of the next words are put in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A display put on by freshly decorated war heroes.
explanation.definitionFit: A raree-show was a peep show carried in a box, hence any spectacle or street show.

clue.text: Author with his subject suggests tea, not cider

definitions.text: Author with his subject suggests tea, not cider

parts.words: Author with his subject suggests tea, not cider
parts.note: Laurie Lee wrote Cider with Rosie; put the girl's name with his surname and the result is rhyming slang for tea

explanation.walkthrough: Rhyming slang: Rosie Lee means tea, in British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Joining the author's surname to his book's heroine gives the Cockney rhyming slang for a cup of tea.

clue.text: Wordsworth had him "blow his wreathed horn"

definitions.text: Wordsworth had him "blow his wreathed horn"

parts.words: Wordsworth had him "blow his wreathed horn"
parts.note: in the sonnet The World Is Too Much With Us, the poet longs to hear a sea-god sound his conch shell

explanation.definitionFit: The Greek sea-god, son of Poseidon, blows a conch shell, which Wordsworth calls his wreathed horn.
